blocks.text: Josiah’s response to the discovered scroll unfolds in public covenant renewal, the removal of prohibited worship, and the celebration of Passover. Yet the chapter deliberately holds this reform beside the narrator’s statement that judgment against Judah will still come because of accumulated provocation. The reform is therefore presented as thorough and significant without being portrayed as canceling that announced judgment.

This chapter stands at a major turn in the movement of 2 Kings: it recounts Judah’s reform under Josiah before the book moves on toward Babylonian destruction and Jehoiachin’s life in exile. That larger movement helps explain why the chapter gives both strong attention to Josiah’s reform and a sober account of what follows.

The account reports that Pharaoh-necoh killed Josiah at Megiddo, but it does not include the speech about Josiah’s decision found in Chronicles. When comparing the accounts, it is important to preserve each account’s distinct wording and purpose rather than quietly supplying details from one into the other.
